messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Editor
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 56

# The Weight of What Was Said

Rajan is twenty-six years old, the kind of man who chose his career because he believes in the precision of language — that the right words, arranged carefully, can clarify the world. He works as an editor at a mid-sized publishing house, spending his days smoothing other people's sentences into something truer than what they first put down. He is good at his job. His colleagues describe him as meticulous, calm, almost unnervingly composed. His wife, Priya, knows a different version of him — the one who wakes at 3 a.m. and cannot explain why.

Eighteen months ago, Rajan was driving home from a late evening at the office when he was pulled over. It was a routine stop, he told himself, though nothing about it felt routine. The officer approached his window with a hand already resting on his belt. Rajan was asked to step out of the car. He complied immediately, speaking carefully, keeping his hands visible, doing everything he understood a person was supposed to do. What followed was twenty minutes during which he was pressed against the hood of his own car, his face turned toward the asphalt, a knee at his back, while a second officer arrived and the two men spoke over him as though he were not there — as though he were not a person at all. No charges were filed. He was eventually told he matched a description. He drove home shaking so badly he had to pull over twice.

In the weeks that followed, Rajan told almost no one. He told Priya a version of it — enough that she understood something had happened, not enough that she understood what it had done to him. He returned to work and sat at his desk and moved words around on a screen, and from the outside, nothing had changed. Inside, everything had.

He began avoiding the route he had taken that night. Then he began avoiding driving after dark altogether. When he sees police vehicles now — even parked, even on television — his body responds before his mind can intervene: his chest tightens, his hands go cold, and a wave of nausea rises that he has learned to breathe through quietly, hoping no one notices. He has become expert at not being noticed.

The dreams come several times a week. In some of them he is back against the hood of the car. In others, the details shift in ways that are worse — he cannot speak, or Priya is there watching, or the scene simply does not end. He wakes with his heart pounding and lies still in the dark, unwilling to move and wake her, running through the logic of where he is and that he is safe, a process that takes longer than it should.

At work, Rajan finds himself reading the same paragraph four and five times without absorbing it. He is irritable in ways he does not recognize in himself — short with junior colleagues over small errors, then privately ashamed. He has stopped attending the informal lunches he used to enjoy. A friend from university visited last month and remarked that Rajan seemed distant. Rajan agreed and changed the subject.

What troubles him most, he admits when he finally speaks about it, is not the fear. It is the shame — the feeling that he handled it wrong, that he should have said something different, been someone different. He is a man who edits for a living, who believes in finding exactly the right words, and he cannot find language for what it meant to be reduced, in those twenty minutes, to something that needed to be managed. He turns this over constantly, the way a tongue finds a sore tooth, pressing again and again on the place that hurts most. Priya watches him disappear into himself at dinner and does not always know how to reach him. He does not always know how to be reached.
